name: Faleolo International Airport
before:
Samoa's international airport, 40 km west of Apia on the island of Upolu. The runway is 3,000 metres and the field sits barely above sea level at 58 feet.

The history explains why the airport matters. Until 1984 it could not take anything bigger than a 737, so flights from the United States, Australia and New Zealand had to land at Pago Pago in American Samoa instead. Once Faleolo was expanded, almost all of Samoa's international traffic moved here.

Its origins are wartime. United States Navy Seabees built the airfield in 1942 alongside a naval base, and a Marine fighter squadron moved in to defend Upolu and Savai'i. After the war it went quiet, serving flying boats on the coral route, and was upgraded for land aircraft in 1957 and again in 1972.

The control tower has an unusually wide brief, covering some of the airspace over American Samoa and Tonga as well as Samoa's own.
after:
Samoa's main international airport, about 40 km west of Apia on the island of Upolu. Its runway is 3,000 metres and the field sits barely above sea level at 58 feet.

The history explains why the airport matters. Until the runway was lengthened for Boeing 747s in 1985, Faleolo could not take the largest jets. Most international traffic to Samoa now comes through here.

Its origins are wartime. United States Navy Seabees built the airfield in 1942 alongside a naval base.

claims.note: The Navy's own history has the runway at Faleolo begun in May 1942 and completed by July 1942, as part of an air base with harbour facilities and seaplane ramps. It credits the 4th Construction Detachment of the 2nd Construction Battalion; Wikipedia says the 1st Battalion, which the text does not name.

claims.claim: 737 limit until 1984; US, Australian and NZ flights landed at Pago Pago
claims.wasBefore: Until 1984 it could not take anything bigger than a 737, so flights from the United States, Australia and New Zealand had to land at Pago Pago in American Samoa instead.
claims.why: The 737 limit and the Pago Pago diversion rest on Wikipedia alone (the authority's timeline starts in 1984 and says nothing of Pago Pago). Softened to the 1985 lengthening for 747s, which both support (see above).

claims.wasBefore: Once Faleolo was expanded, almost all of Samoa's international traffic moved here.

claims.claim: a Marine fighter squadron moved in to defend Upolu and Savai'i
claims.wasBefore: and a Marine fighter squadron moved in to defend Upolu and Savai'i
claims.why: Wikipedia alone. The Marine Corps' own history has VMF-111 operating from Tutuila's airfield, with Navy amphibians sent forward to Upolu while its airfield was rushed to completion; it does not record the move to Faleolo, and the Navy's history does not name a squadron there.
